title: Market hours and extended hours
teaches: When US stocks trade: the 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. ET regular session, pre-market and after hours, why news gaps a stock at the open, and why extended-hours prints are thin and don't set the official close or the consolidated high.

facts.quote: Regular trading hours for stocks traded on exchanges and certain other markets are from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time.
facts.claim: Regular trading hours for US stocks are 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time.

facts.quote: The duration of extended-hours trading sessions varies between markets and trading venues.
facts.claim: How long extended-hours sessions run differs from one market or venue to the next.

facts.quote: However, during extended-hours trading there generally is less trading interest and therefore less price competition for most stocks, which may raise trading costs, increase uncertainty with respect to prevailing prices, or make it more difficult to execute trades.
facts.claim: Extended hours usually have less trading interest and price competition, which can raise costs, blur the real price and make fills harder.

facts.quote: The prices of some stocks traded during extended-hours trading may not reflect the prices of those stocks during regular hours, either at the end of the regular trading session or upon the opening of regular trading the next business day.
facts.claim: An extended-hours price may not match the regular-session close or the next day's open.

facts.quote: Extended-hours trading systems are not linked together. As a result, depending on the extended-hours trading system or the time of day, the price of a stock displayed on one trading system may not reflect the price of the same stock
facts.claim: Extended-hours venues are not linked, so two of them can show different prices for the same stock at the same time.

facts.quote: Companies may announce important news or financial information outside of regular trading hours.
facts.claim: Companies may release important news and financial results outside regular trading hours.

facts.quote: These announcements, combined with other extended-hours trading risks, may lead to significant price changes in these companies’ stocks during extended hours trading.
facts.claim: News released out of hours, on thin trading, can move a stock sharply in extended hours.

facts.quote: The reduced level of trading interest in extended-hours trading generally results in wider spreads between the bid and ask prices for a stock or no quotes at all.
facts.claim: Extended-hours spreads are usually wider, and sometimes there is no quote at all.

facts.quote: With respect to extended-hours trading, many brokerage firms currently accept only limit orders
facts.claim: Many brokers accept only limit orders in extended hours.

facts.quote: For stocks with limited trading activity, investors may find greater price fluctuations than they typically would see during regular trading hours.
facts.claim: Thinly traded stocks can swing more in extended hours than they do in the regular session.

facts.quote: Regular trading hours for listed stocks, as defined by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), are from 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. ET.
facts.claim: FINRA, citing the SEC, puts regular trading hours for listed stocks at 9:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. ET.

facts.quote: Trading activity that takes place early in the morning before regular trading begins is commonly referred to as pre-market trading.
facts.claim: Trading in the morning before the regular session opens is called pre-market trading.

facts.quote: Trading that occurs later in the day after regular trading ends is known as post-market or after-hours trading.
facts.claim: Trading after the regular session ends is called after-hours (or post-market) trading.

facts.quote: Pre-market trading is typically defined as taking place from 7 – 9:30 a.m. ET and after-hours trading from 4 – 8 p.m. ET.
facts.claim: FINRA's typical definition: pre-market 7 to 9:30 a.m. ET, after hours 4 to 8 p.m. ET.

facts.quote: Trading beyond these time periods, such as during the overnight hours from 8 p.m. to 4 a.m. ET, has also more recently been made available to retail investors for certain stocks.
facts.claim: Overnight trading, 8 p.m. to 4 a.m. ET, is now open to retail investors in certain stocks.

facts.quote: Any activity that takes place outside of regular trading hours, whether in the pre-market, after-hours or overnight periods, is generally referred to as extended-hours trading.
facts.claim: Pre-market, after-hours and overnight trading together are called extended-hours trading.

facts.quote: Despite the increasing amount of extended-hours trading activity, that activity is still dwarfed by the tens of millions of transactions that typically take place during regular trading hours.
facts.claim: Extended-hours trading is growing but is still dwarfed by regular-hours trading.

facts.quote: As a result, your order may be executed partially or not at all. If it's executed, it might not be at a competitive price compared to regular trading hours.
facts.claim: In extended hours an order may fill partly or not at all, and a fill may be at a worse price than in regular hours.

facts.quote: Because fewer trades occur during extended hours, stocks might be vulnerable to wider swings.
facts.claim: With fewer trades, stocks can swing more in extended hours.

facts.quote: key corporate events, such as earnings or other significant announcements, which normally take place during the extended-hours period.
facts.claim: Earnings and other big company announcements normally come out during extended hours.

facts.quote: However, trading might become smoother once investors have had time to review and absorb more information about the results and regular trading hours resume.
facts.claim: After an out-of-hours earnings move, trading can settle once people digest the results and the regular session opens.

facts.quote: During regular trading hours, brokerage firms are generally required by SEC rules to fill customer orders for listed stocks at the best price at the time
facts.claim: In regular hours, brokers are generally required to fill orders in listed stocks at the best price available at the time.

facts.quote: However, the NBBO is only published during regular trading hours, so this requirement doesn’t apply to extended-hours trading.
facts.claim: That best-price requirement does not apply in extended hours.

facts.quote: The share prices recorded at 4 p.m. on the exchanges on a given day are considered the official closing prices for that day, regardless of what happens during extended-hours trading.
facts.claim: The 4 p.m. price is the official close, whatever trades in extended hours.

facts.quote: The next day’s opening prices are generated based on supply and demand for the securities at or around the time markets open.
facts.claim: The next day's opening price comes from supply and demand at the open.

facts.quote: Rules among brokerage firms about when and how customers can participate in extended-hours trading may vary.
facts.claim: Each broker sets its own rules for when and how you can trade in extended hours.

facts.quote: For Nasdaq, pre-market trading hours are 4:00 am to 9:30 am, Eastern Time Zone. After hours runs from 4:00 pm to 8:00 pm, Eastern Time Zone.
facts.claim: At Nasdaq, pre-market runs 4:00 to 9:30 a.m. ET and after hours runs 4:00 to 8:00 p.m. ET.

facts.quote: Certain brokers have different pre-market and after hours trading times.
facts.claim: Some brokers use different extended-hours times than the exchange.

facts.quote: The volatility tends to be much higher, and there is less liquidity, meaning that fewer people are trading and that prices tend to move much more dramatically.
facts.claim: Extended hours have higher volatility and less liquidity: fewer people trading and bigger price moves.

facts.quote: Thanksgiving Day November 26, 2026 Closed Early Close November 27, 2026 1:00 p.m.
facts.claim: Nasdaq's 2026 calendar: closed Thanksgiving, November 26, and an early close at 1:00 p.m. on November 27.

facts.quote: Currently the Nasdaq stock market operates from 4:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET.
facts.claim: Today the Nasdaq Stock Market runs from 4:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET, extended hours included.

facts.quote: The U.S. trading hours, from 9:30 a.m. - 4:00 p.m. ET and marked by the Opening and Closing Crosses, will continue to set the prices to drive investor transparency across all hours of market operation.
facts.claim: Even with longer hours, the 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. session and its opening and closing auctions keep setting the reference prices.

facts.quote: On December 6, 2026, the Nasdaq Stock Market will introduce new trading hours from 9:00 pm-4:00 am ET.
facts.claim: Nasdaq plans to add a 9:00 p.m. to 4:00 a.m. ET session from December 6, 2026.

facts.quote: The Opening Cross sets the Nasdaq Official Opening Price (NOOP).
facts.claim: Nasdaq's opening auction (the Opening Cross) sets the official opening price.

facts.quote: The Closing Cross sets the Nasdaq Official Closing Price (NOCP).
facts.claim: Nasdaq's closing auction (the Closing Cross) sets the official closing price.

facts.quote: At 4:00 p.m., the Closing Cross is initiated and the on-close book and the continuous book are brought together to create a single Nasdaq Closing Cross.
facts.claim: Nasdaq's Closing Cross runs at 4:00 p.m.

facts.quote: Regular Hours orders are executable from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.
facts.claim: At Nasdaq, a regular-hours order can execute only from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

facts.quote: Extended Hours orders are executable from 4:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.
facts.claim: At Nasdaq, an order marked for extended hours can execute from 4:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.

facts.quote: Each market will close early at 1:00 p.m. (1:15 p.m. for eligible options) on Friday, November 27, 2026, Friday, November 26, 2027, and Friday, November 24, 2028 (the day after Thanksgiving).
facts.claim: NYSE markets close early, at 1:00 p.m. ET, on the day after Thanksgiving: Friday, November 27, 2026.

facts.quote: Core Trading Session: 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. ET 9:30 a.m. ET - Core Open Auction 3:50 p.m. to 4:00 p.m. ET - Closing Imbalance Period 4:00 p.m. ET - Closing Auction
facts.claim: On the NYSE the core session runs 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. ET, opening with an auction at 9:30 and closing with one at 4:00.

facts.quote: Trades executed during the Overnight, Early and Late Sessions will use the ‘T’ sale condition and will not be Last Sale eligible.
facts.claim: On NYSE Arca, trades outside the core session are flagged 'T' and do not count as the last sale.

facts.quote: Will extended hours trading count toward the consolidated volume? A: Yes.
facts.claim: Extended-hours trades count toward consolidated volume.

facts.quote: NYSE Arca will continue to publish the OCP following the Core Closing Auction at 4:00 PM
facts.claim: NYSE Arca publishes its official closing price after its 4:00 p.m. closing auction.

facts.quote: 3.14.2 UTP Sale Condition Matrix Consolidated Processing Guidelines Market Center Processing Guidelines Modifier Condition Update High/Low Update Last Update High/Low Update Last Update Volume
facts.claim: The UTP Plan's sale-condition table says, for each kind of trade, whether it updates the consolidated high/low, the last price and the volume.

facts.quote: T Form T No No No No Yes
facts.claim: In that table a Form T trade updates volume only: not the high/low and not the last price.

facts.quote: The Form T (T) Sale Condition should be applied for the following: • Trades executed on trade day between 12:00 a.m. and 9:30 a.m. • Trades executed on trade day between 4:00:01 p.m. and 8:00 p.m.
facts.claim: Form T marks trades from midnight to 9:30 a.m. and from just after 4:00 p.m. to 8:00 p.m.

facts.quote: Denotes the sale condition associated with a trade. Also noted is the impact of Sale Conditions on the Open, Last, High and Low calculations both on a Consolidated and Participant basis.
facts.claim: The CTA's trade feed lists how each sale condition affects the open, last, high and low.

facts.quote: T Extended Hours Trade NO NO NO NO NO YES
facts.claim: In the CTA table an extended-hours trade updates volume only, not the last, high or low.

facts.quote: Extended Hours Trade Identifies a trade that was executed outside of regular primary market hours and is reported as an extended hours trade.
facts.claim: An 'extended hours trade' is one executed outside regular market hours.

facts.quote: Trades executed outside Regular Trading Hours (9:30 AM – 4:00 PM) will continue to use the 'T' sale condition and are not Last Sale eligible.
facts.claim: Trades outside 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. carry the 'T' condition and are not last-sale eligible, before and after the longer hours start.

facts.quote: Yes. Trades executed during ETH are included in consolidated volume totals as per the Sale Conditions eligibility.
facts.claim: Extended-hours trades are included in consolidated volume.

facts.quote: The stop price is a trigger that causes the stop order to become a market order.
facts.claim: Hitting the stop price turns a stop order into a market order.

facts.quote: The execution price an investor receives for this market order can deviate significantly from the stop price due to the demand for a stock and the prices of available liquidity.
facts.claim: A triggered stop can fill far from the stop price.

facts.quote: Day orders, if not executed, generally cancel at the end of regular trading hours of the trading day that they are entered and will not carry over to the extended hours session or the next trading day.
facts.claim: An unfilled day order generally cancels at the end of regular hours and does not carry into extended hours or the next day.

facts.quote: if you place your order before or after normal trading hours, consider the possibility that news events or other factors might significantly impact the price of the security when the market opens again.
facts.claim: News that comes out while the market is closed can move the price a long way by the next open.

facts.quote: When this stop price is reached, the order automatically turns into a market order and is executed as soon as possible at the current market price.
facts.claim: A triggered stop fills as soon as possible at the current market price.

facts.quote: Orders for the premarket session can be placed from 7:00 a.m. to 9:28 a.m. ET. Orders in the after-hours session can be placed from 4:00 p.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET.
facts.claim: Fidelity's pre-market runs 7:00 to 9:28 a.m. ET and its after hours 4:00 to 8:00 p.m. ET.

facts.quote: Fidelity will accept limit orders in the extended-hours trading sessions; all other order types are ineligible for trading during extended-hours.
facts.claim: Fidelity takes only limit orders in extended hours.

facts.quote: There is no Reg NMS trade through protection during the extended-hours sessions, so price/time priority is set by each market center, not across market centers.
facts.claim: In extended hours there is no protection against trading through a better price on another venue.

facts.quote: Keep in mind that news stories and related announcements, coupled with lower liquidity and higher volatility, may cause an exaggerated and unsustainable effect on the price of a security.
facts.claim: News on thin, volatile extended-hours trading can push a price further than it holds.

facts.quote: Extended trading allows for buying and selling stocks before markets open and after markets close, but rules vary by brokerage firm.
facts.claim: You can trade before the open and after the close, but the rules depend on your broker.

facts.quote: The vast majority of trading occurs during normal business hours, meaning that there is more demand for stock you are selling, and more supply of stock you want to buy.
facts.claim: Most trading happens in regular hours, which is where buyers and sellers are deepest.

facts.quote: Because many public companies release quarterly earnings after 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time, investors have the opportunity to immediately place a trade following an announcement
facts.claim: Many companies report earnings after 4:00 p.m. ET, so the first reaction trades after hours.

facts.quote: Pre-market session: 7:00 a.m. to 9:25 a.m.
facts.claim: Schwab's pre-market session runs 7:00 to 9:25 a.m. ET.

facts.quote: After-hours session: 4:05 p.m. to 8:00 p.m.
facts.claim: Schwab's after-hours session runs 4:05 to 8:00 p.m. ET.

facts.quote: Stop orders will not be eligible for execution during an extended hours session.
facts.claim: At Schwab, stop orders do not execute in extended hours.

facts.quote: Extended hours trading sessions are completely independent from the regular trading sessions, and you must specify which type of trading session (regular or extended) you intend for your order.
facts.claim: At Schwab you must mark an order for the regular or the extended session; they are separate.

facts.quote: Unlike the regular session, extended-hours trading accepts only limit orders.
facts.claim: Schwab's extended-hours sessions accept only limit orders.

facts.quote: With fewer participants trading, a single order can move a security's price more than it might during regular hours, leading to sharper swings.
facts.claim: With fewer people trading, one order can move the price more than it would in regular hours.

facts.quote: Many companies release earnings after the close of the regular session.
facts.claim: Many companies report earnings after the regular close.

facts.quote: Price charts often have blank spaces known as gaps, representing times when no shares were traded within a particular price range. Usually this occurs between the market close and the next trading day's open.
facts.claim: A gap is a blank space on the chart where no shares traded, usually between one day's close and the next day's open.

facts.quote: Gaps result from extraordinary buying or selling interests often developing while the market is closed. For example, if an unexpectedly strong earnings report comes out after the market has closed, a lot of buying interest will be generated overnight.
facts.claim: Gaps come from buying or selling that builds while the market is closed, such as after a strong earnings report.

facts.quote: A gap is a change in price levels between the close and open of two consecutive days.
facts.claim: A gap is measured from one day's close to the next day's open.

facts.quote: Trade-through means the purchase or sale of an NMS stock during regular trading hours, either as principal or agent, at a price that is lower than a protected bid or higher than a protected offer.
facts.claim: The SEC's trade-through rule, which stops a trade at a worse price than another venue's protected quote, covers regular trading hours only.

facts.quote: In the regular session, stock quotes are consolidated and represent the best available prices across all trading venues.
facts.claim: In regular hours, consolidated quotes combine the best prices from every trading venue.

walkthroughs.title: Three sessions, one clock
steps: The regular session runs 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time. That's where most of the trading happens.
Before it is pre-market. After it is after hours. Some stocks now trade overnight too. All of it is extended hours.
At Nasdaq, pre-market starts at 4:00 a.m. and after hours runs to 8:00 p.m.
Your broker sets its own window. Fidelity and Schwab start pre-market at 7:00 a.m.

walkthroughs.title: Thin prints and official prints
steps: Outside regular hours, far fewer people trade. Spreads widen and one order can swing the price.
Those trades carry a T flag. They add to the day's volume.
But the consolidated record, which combines every venue, leaves them out of the day's high, low and last.
The official open and close normally come from the auctions. The close is the 4 p.m. price, whatever trades later.

walkthroughs.title: Why gaps show up at the open
steps: Earnings and other big company news usually come out while the regular session is closed.
The stock reprices on thin after-hours and pre-market trading. The open can land far from yesterday's close. That jump is the gap.
Many brokers take only limit orders outside regular hours. At those brokers, a stop waits for the open.
Once hit, a stop becomes a market order. It fills at the going price, which can be far from your stop.

questions.q: What are regular trading hours for US stocks?
questions.why: 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time. That's the regular session, as the SEC and FINRA define it.
questions.lesson_line: The session is 9:30 to 4:00 Eastern. Anything outside it is extended hours.

wrong.9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. your time: The clock is Eastern Time wherever you live. Convert it to your own time zone.
wrong.4:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET: That's Nasdaq's pre-market start to its after-hours end. The regular session is only the middle of it.
wrong.9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. ET: Those are office hours. The regular session opens at 9:30 a.m. and closes at 4:00 p.m.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Trading in the hours just before the 9:30 a.m. open is called ___ trading.
questions.why: Pre-market. FINRA uses that name for trading early in the morning, before regular trading begins.
questions.lesson_line: Pre-market comes before the open. After hours comes after the close.

questions.q: Most of a normal day's stock trading happens outside regular hours.
questions.why: False. FINRA says extended-hours activity is still dwarfed by regular-hours trading. Fidelity says the vast majority happens in the regular session.
questions.lesson_line: The crowd trades 9:30 to 4:00. Outside those hours you're in a much thinner market.

questions.q: When do companies usually release their earnings reports?
questions.why: Outside regular trading hours. FINRA says earnings and other big announcements normally come out in the extended-hours period.
questions.lesson_line: Big news lands while the regular session is shut. That's when the stock starts to reprice.

wrong.During regular trading hours: Not usually. Many companies report after the 4:00 p.m. close, so the first reaction trades after hours.
wrong.Right at the 9:30 a.m. open: The news usually comes out outside the session, not at the bell. By the open it's already out.

questions.q: Every broker lets you trade from 4:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET.
questions.why: False. Nasdaq's extended hours run 4:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m., but brokers set their own windows. Fidelity and Schwab start pre-market at 7:00 a.m.
questions.lesson_line: The exchange's hours are not your hours. Check what your broker allows.

questions.q: Outside regular hours, many brokers accept only one order type. Which one?
questions.why: Limit orders. The SEC notes many brokers take only limit orders in extended hours. Fidelity and Schwab both work that way.
questions.lesson_line: Out of hours, name your price. A limit order is usually the only order that works.

wrong.Market orders: Those are what brokers keep out. With thin trading, a market order could fill far from the price you saw.
wrong.Stop orders: Schwab says stop orders aren't eligible in extended hours, and Fidelity takes limit orders only.
wrong.Stop-limit orders: A stop-limit isn't a plain limit order. Schwab and Fidelity take only limit orders out of hours.

questions.q: Regular hours only, how many 5-minute bars make one full trading day?
questions.why: 78. The session runs 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., six and a half hours. Cut that into 5-minute bars.
questions.lesson_line: Count more than 78 five-minute bars in a full day and your chart is showing extended hours.

questions.q: A 5-minute bar on your chart is stamped 4:35 p.m. ET. Which session is it from?
questions.why: After hours. The regular session ends at 4:00 p.m. ET, and Nasdaq's after-hours session runs to 8:00 p.m.
questions.lesson_line: Read the time stamp first. From 4:00 to 8:00 p.m. ET, you're looking at thinner after-hours trading.

wrong.Regular session: The regular session ends at 4:00 p.m. ET. This bar comes after the close.
wrong.Pre-market: Pre-market is the morning, before the 9:30 a.m. open.
wrong.Overnight: FINRA puts overnight hours at 8 p.m. to 4 a.m. ET. This bar comes earlier.

questions.q: Friday, November 27, 2026 is the day after Thanksgiving. When does the regular session end?
questions.why: 1:00 p.m. ET. The NYSE and Nasdaq both list that Friday as an early close.
questions.lesson_line: Check the holiday calendar each year. A half day ends at 1:00 p.m. ET.

wrong.4:00 p.m. ET: That's a normal day. This Friday is a half day, with an early close at 1:00 p.m.
wrong.It's closed all day: Thanksgiving itself, Thursday, November 26, is the full holiday. Friday trades, then closes early.

questions.story: A stock closes at $60 on Tuesday. At 4:05 p.m. it reports earnings far above forecasts. On Wednesday it opens at $66.
questions.q: What caused the gap at Wednesday's open?
choices: News that came out after the close
The after-hours price became the close
The exchange reset the price overnight
questions.answer: News that came out after the close
questions.why: News that came out after the close. Buying built up overnight, so the stock opened well above Tuesday's close. That jump is the gap.
questions.lesson_line: A gap is often news the regular session never got to trade. Expect them around earnings.

wrong.The after-hours price became the close: The close stays Tuesday's 4 p.m. price. After-hours trades don't change it.
wrong.The exchange reset the price overnight: Nobody sets it by hand. The open comes from supply and demand at the open.

questions.q: A stock trades at $80.00 at 4:00 p.m. At 6:30 p.m. it trades at $83.00. What is the day's official close?
questions.why: $80.00. The 4 p.m. price is the official close, whatever happens in extended hours. On Nasdaq, the Closing Cross sets it.
questions.lesson_line: After-hours prints are real trades. The close is still the 4:00 p.m. price.

wrong.$83.00: That's an after-hours trade. FINRA says extended hours don't change the official close.
After hours can run to 8:00 p.m., but the official close was set at 4:00 p.m.

questions.q: Yesterday's close was $40.00. This morning it opens at $44.00. How big is the gap, as a percent of the close?
questions.why: 10%. Take the open minus the close, then divide by the close.
questions.lesson_line: Measure a gap from yesterday's close to today's open, in percent.

questions.story: At 3:58 p.m. you place a day limit order to sell at $25.00. It doesn't fill by the 4:00 p.m. close. At 4:30 p.m. the stock trades at $25.20.
questions.q: What most likely happened to your order?
choices: It cancelled at the 4:00 p.m. close
questions.answer: It cancelled at the 4:00 p.m. close
questions.why: It cancelled at the close. A plain day order generally ends with regular trading hours. It doesn't carry into after hours or the next day.
questions.lesson_line: To trade after the bell, mark the order for extended hours. A plain day order stops at the close.

wrong.It sold at $25.20 after hours: A plain day order doesn't carry into extended hours. You have to pick that session on the order.
wrong.It waits for tomorrow's open: A day order is good for one day. It won't carry over to the next trading day.

questions.q: After hours, your broker must still fill you at the best price shown across all venues.
questions.why: False. FINRA says the best-price requirement doesn't apply to extended hours. Venues aren't linked then, so one can show a worse price than another.
questions.lesson_line: Out of hours you get the price where your order lands, not the best price anywhere.

questions.story: At 7:40 a.m. ET a stock prints $26.00. It closed yesterday at $24.00. Only a few hundred shares have traded so far.
questions.q: How should you read that $26.00 print?
choices: A thin print that may not hold
The price it will open at
A cue to buy at market now
questions.answer: A thin print that may not hold
questions.why: A thin print that may not hold. With few shares trading, one order can move the price. Extended-hours prices may not match regular-hours prices.
questions.lesson_line: I treat a 7:40 a.m. print as a hint, not a verdict. The open is the real test.

wrong.The price it will open at: Not promised. The SEC warns extended-hours prices may not reflect prices in regular hours.
wrong.A cue to buy at market now: Many brokers take only limit orders this early. Thin trading can also raise what you pay.

questions.q: Shares traded in the pre-market count toward a stock's consolidated volume for the day.
questions.why: True. Extended-hours trades are included in consolidated volume. The NYSE and the CTA plan both say so, and the UTP table marks them yes for volume.
questions.lesson_line: Big pre-market volume is real volume. It counts in the day's total.

questions.q: A trade at 7:40 a.m. can set a stock's consolidated high for the day.
questions.why: False. Trades outside 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. carry a T condition. In both consolidated data plans they update volume, not the high, low or last.
questions.lesson_line: A pre-market high is a real trade, but it doesn't set the day's consolidated high.

questions.story: You own a stock that closed at $50, with a sell stop at $48. Your broker runs stops in regular hours only. Weak earnings after the close send it to $42. It opens next morning at $43.
questions.q: Where does your stop most likely fill?
questions.why: Near $43, just after the open. The stop triggers in the regular session and becomes a market order. It fills near where the stock trades, not at $48.
questions.lesson_line: A stop can't catch an overnight gap. News can open the stock right through it.

wrong.At $48, your stop price: The stop price is a trigger, not a promised fill. The stock opened below it.
wrong.Near $42, in after hours: Your broker doesn't run stops after hours, so nothing triggered until the regular session.

questions.story: You hold a stock into earnings. It reports at 4:05 p.m. and falls 9% after hours. The quote is wide, and only small trades are printing.
questions.q: What's the most accurate read right now?
choices: Real news, but a thin, shaky price
The official close is now 9% lower
questions.answer: Real news, but a thin, shaky price
questions.why: Real news, but a thin, shaky price. Extended-hours prices may not match the next open. FINRA notes trading can settle once regular hours resume.
questions.lesson_line: Respect the news, not the exact after-hours price. The open is where the full market weighs in.

wrong.The official close is now 9% lower: The close is still the 4 p.m. price. After-hours trading doesn't change it.
wrong.It will open 9% lower tomorrow: Not a given. The SEC warns extended-hours prices may not reflect the next day's open.

conflicts: When pre-market starts: FINRA says pre-market is 'typically' 7 to 9:30 a.m. ET (f14); Nasdaq's pre-market starts at 4:00 a.m. (f27); NYSE Arca's early session starts at 4:00 a.m. and NYSE American, National and Texas start at 7:00 a.m. (NYSE hours page); Fidelity and Schwab start at 7:00 a.m. (f57, f64). No question keys one start time for pre-market in general. Every time in a question names the venue or the broker, and q05 teaches that windows differ.

Longer hours are coming: Nasdaq (f33, 23/5 hub) and NYSE Arca (NYSE extended-hours FAQ, August 2026) plan a 9:00 p.m. to 4:00 a.m. ET overnight session from December 6, 2026, four weeks after as_of, pending SEC approvals and SIP readiness; the CTA FAQ (v1.2) gives the same date. Nothing in this unit says trading stops at 8:00 p.m. or that no overnight trading exists. The regular session, its opening and closing auctions (f32) and the 'T' / not-last-sale rule (f50) are unchanged by the plan. Re-read the Nasdaq hub and FINRA's page after December 6, 2026.

Best price after hours (q14): FINRA's page (accessed 2026-11-08) says the NBBO is only published in regular hours, so the best-price requirement doesn't apply in extended hours (f23). The SIPs move to about 23 hours from December 6, 2026 (CTA FAQ), so the 'NBBO is only published' half may change. The key rests on the requirement not applying out of hours, which Fidelity also states as no Reg NMS trade-through protection in extended sessions (f59). The why does not repeat the 'only published' clause.

Day orders (q13): Investor.gov says day orders 'generally' cancel at the end of regular hours (f54); some brokers sell day orders that include extended hours (Schwab's 'Day + Extended'). The story says 'a day limit order' and the question asks what 'most likely' happened.

Stops after hours (q18, w3): the SEC says 'many' brokers take only limit orders in extended hours (f9); Fidelity (f58) and Schwab (f66, f68) don't run stops then, but not every broker is the same. The q18 story states the broker's rule.

Consolidated high (q17): both consolidated data plans agree that 'T' trades update volume only (UTP f45, CTA f48). The question says 'consolidated high', which is what those tables govern. A chart vendor can still draw extended-hours bars its own way, so no question claims what a member's chart shows beyond q07's arithmetic (regular hours only, 78 five-minute bars).

Schwab's own pages give different counts for overnight-eligible securities (over 1,300 on the extended-hours page, other figures elsewhere). Not used. Schwab's learn article cites NYSE for extended hours at 'over 11%' of share volume in early 2025; not used (one Tier 2 publisher citing a page not read here). q03 rests on FINRA (f17) and Fidelity (f62) instead.
Fidelity's Viewpoints article says the jobs report comes out 'on the first Friday of every month'; the BLS schedule shows some releases on other Fridays. Not used.
Overlap with F1.03: F1.03 q18 already asks which order to use after hours on a wide quote. This unit does not ask it again; q06 asks which order type brokers accept, a different fact.

Two senses of 'gap' (checker, 2026-11-09): StockCharts' gaps article (s18) calls a gap a blank space on the chart, and an up gap needs the day's low to stay above the prior high; its gap-trading article (s19) measures close to open and calls an open above yesterday's high a 'full gap'. q10, q12 and w3 use the close-to-open sense (f73). No question asks whether a gap filled or whether the range cleared the prior day.

q14 after December 6, 2026 (checker): the SIPs move to about 23 hours, so FINRA's 'the NBBO is only published during regular trading hours' may change. Reg NMS Rule 600(b)(105) (f74, eCFR up to date as of 11/05/2026) defines a trade-through as one 'during regular trading hours', so trade-through protection still stops at 4:00 p.m. unless the rule changes. Best execution (a broker's duty of care) still applies out of hours; q14 is about a best price across venues, which no rule promises then. Re-read FINRA's page and Rule 600 after December 6, 2026.
Early-close days (q09): NYSE's hours page says NYSE American, Arca, National and Texas late sessions close at 5:00 p.m. ET on early-close days. q09 asks only when the regular session ends.

Cross-unit overlap, for the owner (checker, 2026-11-09; those units were not yet checked): F11.01 q10 asks the same 78 five-minute-bars sum as q07; V.07 q29 has the same shape as q13 (day limit order, unfilled at the close, a later after-hours price); F5.04 q20 and F5.06 q07 teach the stop-through-a-gap idea of q18 and w3; F5.04 q08 and F5.07 q07 teach the after-hours-price-vs-open idea of q15 and q19. F1.05 is the hours unit, so it is the natural home; pick one home per idea or accept the repeat as review.

w1.notes: Re-read f1, f17, f12, f13, f16 (SEC, FINRA), f27 (Nasdaq hours page), f57 (Fidelity FAQ; Fidelity Viewpoints agrees: pre-market 'entered and executed between 7:00 a.m. and 9:28 a.m.') and f64 (Schwab) on fresh pages, 2026-11-09. Step 2 now adds 'Some stocks now trade overnight too' (f15), so q08's 'Overnight' choice is taught first, and 'All of it is extended hours' matches FINRA f16.

w2.notes: f17, f8, f69 confirmed. Read the UTP matrix (spec p.48: Form T No/No/No/No, volume Yes) and the CTA table (spec p.82: T NO x5, volume YES) page by page. Step 2 said T trades 'don't set the day's high, low or last' flatly, but charts can still draw them, so it now names the consolidated record, explained with Schwab's own words (new f75). Split into 4 steps to fit 22 words. Step 4 now says 'normally': per the Nasdaq FAQ, a stock with no cross takes its last regular trade.

w3.notes: f20, f6, f72, f73, f9, f66, f52, f56 confirmed. 'Big news' would cover Fed decisions, which come out during the session, so it now says 'big company news' (FINRA f20). 'The open lands far' is now 'can land far'. 'A stop sleeps until the regular session' was stated for every broker, but f9 says 'many', so it now says 'At those brokers'. Added step 4 (f53): a triggered stop can fill far from the stop price.

q01.notes: f1 (SEC) and f11 (FINRA) confirmed. The note on '4:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.' called it 'Nasdaq's whole day'. Nasdaq's 23/5 hub adds a 9 p.m. to 4 a.m. session from Dec 6, 2026, so that line would go stale. It now says 'pre-market start to its after-hours end' (f27, f31). The other notes are right.

q02.notes: f12 (FINRA) confirmed. Only 'pre-market' fits 'just before the 9:30 a.m. open'. Overnight is 8 p.m. to 4 a.m. (f15), and 'core' is NYSE's name for the regular session (f40), so both are real mix-ups. No change.

q03.notes: f17 (FINRA: extended-hours activity 'still dwarfed' by regular hours) and f62 (Fidelity: 'vast majority' in normal hours) confirmed in context. Two publishers, and a Tier 1 source among them. No change.

q04.notes: f20 (FINRA: earnings 'normally take place during the extended-hours period'), f70 (Schwab) and f63 (Fidelity) confirmed. Both wrong notes are right. No change.

q05.notes: f27 (Nasdaq 4:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.), f28, and f57 / f64 (Fidelity and Schwab pre-market from 7:00 a.m.) confirmed. Schwab's 24/5 list on thinkorswim does not make 'every broker' true. No change.

q06.notes: f9 (SEC: 'many brokerage firms currently accept only limit orders'), f58 (Fidelity) and f66, f68 (Schwab, article dated Sept 21, 2026) confirmed. Each wrong note matches its source. A different fact from F1.03 q18. No change.

q07.notes: Recomputed by hand: 4:00 p.m. minus 9:30 a.m. is 6.5 h = 390 min, and 390 / 5 = 78. The calc agrees. The lesson holds: a full regular day cannot show more than 78 five-minute bars. F11.01 q10 asks the same sum (see conflicts). No change.

q08.notes: f1 and f27 confirmed. 4:35 p.m. is after hours whether a platform stamps a bar's start or its end. The lesson line said any print 'after 4:00 p.m.' is after hours, but after 8:00 p.m. it is overnight (f15). It now says 4:00 to 8:00 p.m. ET (f27), with f17 added for 'thinner'.

q09.notes: NYSE hours page: 'close early at 1:00 p.m. ... on Friday, November 27, 2026' (f39). Nasdaq's 2026 calendar shows the same early close, with Thanksgiving (Nov 26) closed (f30). NYSE's late sessions close at 5:00 p.m. that day, but the question asks only about the regular session (see conflicts). No change.

q10.notes: f72, f71, f24, f25 confirmed. The question said 'the gap on Wednesday's daily bar', but a gap sits between bars, so it now asks about 'the gap at Wednesday's open' (s19's close-to-open sense). The key said 'while the market was shut', which clashes with the after-hours session this unit teaches. It now says 'News that came out after the close' (f72). The lesson line now says 'often', because gaps also happen without news.

q11.notes: f24 (FINRA: 4 p.m. prices are the official close 'regardless of what happens during extended-hours trading'), f35 and f36 confirmed. The question said 'closes at $80.00', which gave the answer away. It now says 'trades at $80.00 at 4:00 p.m.'

q12.notes: Recomputed: (44 - 40) / 40 = 10%, and pct_change agrees. The close-to-open gap matches StockCharts s19 (f73). No change.

q13.notes: f54 (Investor.gov: day orders 'generally cancel at the end of regular trading hours' and 'will not carry over to the extended hours session or the next trading day') confirmed. 'Most likely' covers brokers' Day + Extended orders (Schwab f67). Same shape as V.07 q29 (see conflicts). No change.

q14.notes: f22, f23 (FINRA), f5 (SEC) and f59 (Fidelity) confirmed. Added f74, Reg NMS Rule 600(b)(105) (eCFR, up to date as of 11/05/2026): a trade-through is one 'during regular trading hours', so False still holds after the SIPs extend their hours on Dec 6, 2026. Best execution still applies, but the statement claims a best price across venues, which nothing guarantees then.

q15.notes: f4, f69, f9, f18 confirmed. f4 compares extended-hours prices with regular-hours prices. The why and the 'open at' note had narrowed that to 'the open', so both now say regular-hours prices, as the SEC does. The key and the lesson are sound trading sense: a thin print is a hint, not a verdict.

q16.notes: UTP matrix: Form T updates volume (f45) and covers trades from 12:00 a.m. to 9:30 a.m. (f46, now cited). CTA table: T volume YES (f48, now cited). The NYSE and CTA FAQs both say yes (f42, f51). 'Before 9:30 a.m.' could include the previous evening's overnight trades, so it now says 'in the pre-market'.

q17.notes: Read the UTP matrix (p.48) and the CTA table (p.82): T trades update neither the consolidated high/low nor the last. Form T covers 12:00 a.m. to 9:30 a.m. (f46), so 7:40 a.m. falls inside it. 'Consolidated' is now taught in w2. In the lesson line, 'doesn't print' is now 'doesn't set'.

q18.notes: f52, f53 (SEC), f56 (FINRA) and f66 (Schwab) confirmed. The story states the broker's rule, so the key, near $43 just after the open, holds, and both wrong notes are right. Same idea as F5.04 q20 (see conflicts). No change.

q19.notes: f21, f4, f24, f19, f8 confirmed. The key respects the news without promising a rebound. The wrong notes match f24 and f4. Close to q15 but adds 'the news is real' and the official close. No change.
